And after sitting with those words for a long time, I realized Naomi was absolutely right.” I was sitting in front of a room full of students at a youth empowerment camp on the Arizona-Mexico border when a disability justice advocate named Naomi Ortiz looked at me and said, calmly but directly, “What you’re doing isn’t helpful, Spencer.” I had just finished describing my proudest professional achievement: summiting Mount Kilimanjaro on my hands and in my wheelchair while raising over half a million dollars for clean water in East Africa. I thought I was inspiring these kids. I thought I was proof of what was possible. “It’s great you climbed Kilimanjaro,” they said, “but you accomplished this because you had a team of people helping you. And through this experience, you supported them to learn and grow as well, which is interdependence.” “You’re what we call a ‘super crip,’” they told me. “A super crip is someone who acts like they can overcome who they are, but a lot of disabled people can’t actually do that. As a public figure, sharing how you accomplished this climb as a team can help others understand that when we come together, we often succeed.” My mouth was on the floor. WE asked Sun readers for their thoughts on the PM cutting pensions to fund a care service – and the results were overwhelming. Andy Burnham announced he would be scrapping the pension triple lock in order to pay for his new social care service, billed as free at the point of use. Currently the triple lock currently guarantees the annual state pension will increase by inflation , 2.5 per cent or average yearly earnings, whichever is higher. But the PM said at his first Labour conference speech that from 2030 it will no longer be linked to average earnings. items.key: ai:nvidia is buying back shares—here's what stock buybacks mean for investors
items.text: Nvidia is buying back shares—here’s what stock buybacks mean for investors
items.article: A buyback can tell investors how a company is using its cash, but not necessarily whether it's a good investment. Nvidia added $150 billion to its share buyback program on Monday , an increase the firm says is the largest in history. The chipmaker now plans to buy back $235 billion worth of stock through January 2028. But what does it actually mean for an investor when a company buys back its own stock? Companies typically buy back shares when they have excess cash, often purchasing their own stock on the open market. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC's "Squawk Box" the company expects to generate "a lot of cash in the coming years" and wants to return some of it to shareholders. Indeed, buybacks, like dividends, are viewed as a way companies can give back to those who invest in their stock. Unlike a dividend, which comes directly to shareholders in the form of cash, a buyback reduces the number of shares in circulation, leaving existing shareholders with a slightly larger piece of the company. Nvidia's announcement comes as share buybacks remain near record levels. But whether a buyback announcement is good news for investors isn't always straightforward. "A buyback is a receipt, not a reason to buy," says Aaron Gaines, a certified financial planner with Gaines Capital Management in Georgia. A buyback announcement only tells you that management intends to spend the company's cash on its own stock, not "whether they got a good deal."
